3. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)






NoteA loss function ?



If we accept that we cannot perfectily fit all data points, what would be the best compromise? How should we measures a distance from optimal fit? Can we invent a single number?




Python Code: Baseline Model & Residual Errors
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)
n = 100
x = np.random.uniform(10, 80, n)
y = 20 + 1.8 * x + np.random.normal(0, 12, n)
y_mean = np.mean(y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.8), dpi=300)
ax.vlines(x, y_mean, y, colors='#d62728', linestyles='--', linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.6, zorder=2, label='Errors ($e_i$)')
ax.scatter(x, y, color='#d62728', alpha=0.5, edgecolors='k', linewidth=0.5, zorder=3, label='Data')
ax.axhline(y_mean, color='#1f77b4', linewidth=2, zorder=4, label='Mean Model ($\\bar{y}$)')

ax.set_xlabel('Carbohydrate intake [g]', fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel('Blood glucose response [mg/dL]', fontsize=11)
ax.set_title('Baseline Model (Mean Blood Glucose) & Residual Errors', fontsize=12, pad=12)
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
ax.legend(loc='lower right', frameon=True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









We define the Residual Sum of Squares \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\) as the squared \(L_2\) norm of the error vector \(e\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{RSS}(\theta) &= \|e\|^2 = e^T e = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 \\
&= (y - X\theta)^T (y - X\theta) \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad \text{minimize}
\end{aligned}\]
Notice that RSS is a simple number (a scalar product).



Deriving the OLS Estimator
To find the optimal parameter vector \(\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}}\), we minimize \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\) by setting its gradient to zero:






NoteStep-by-Step Derivation






Expand the Residual Sum of Squares \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\): \[\begin{aligned}
\text{RSS}(\theta) &= e^T e = (y - X\theta)^T (y - X\theta) \\
&= y^T y - y^T X \theta - \theta^T X^T y + \theta^T X^T X \theta \\
&= y^T y - 2 \theta^T X^T y + \theta^T X^T X \theta
\end{aligned}\]
Notice: \(y^T X \theta = \theta^T X^T y\) is a scalar.
Compute the gradient vector with respect to \(\theta\): \[\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta \text{RSS}(\theta) &= -2 X^T y + 2 X^T X \theta \\
&= -2 X^T (y - X\theta) = -2 X^T e
\end{aligned}\]
Notice: \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\) is a scalar and the gradient \(\nabla_\theta \text{RSS}(\theta)\) has the same dimensions as \(\theta\)
Set the gradient to zero (First-Order Necessary Condition): \[-2 X^T e = 0 \iff X^T X \theta = X^T y \quad \text{(Normal Equations)}\]
Solve for \(\theta\) assuming \(C = X^T X\) is invertible: \[\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} = C^{-1} X^T y \quad \text{where } C = X^T X\]
Dimensions Summary: \[\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}, \quad C = X^T X \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, \quad C^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, \quad X^T \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times n}, \quad y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\]
Notice: for our motivating example \(n=100\) and \(p=2\)




\[\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\]

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
4. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

Probabilistic Modeling of Noise
\[y_i = x_i^T \theta + e_i\]
Assume residual errors \(e_i\) are independent Gaussian noise: \[e_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \implies y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(x_i^T \theta, \sigma^2)\]



The Likelihood Function \(L(\theta)\)
Assuming the model is correct, the probability of a single observation \(y_i\) is:
\[p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)\]
Assuming independent observations, the joint likelihood of observing all \(n\) patient responses is the product over all observations:
\[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)\]



Maximizing Log-Likelihood
Taking the natural log turns the product into a sum:
\[\ell(\theta) = \ln L(\theta) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2\]
Maximizing \(\ell(\theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\):
\[\arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta) \iff \arg\min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2 = \arg\min_\theta \|y - X\theta\|^2\]

Takeaway: Under Gaussian noise, Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) yields the exact same estimator as OLS!

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
5. Geometric Derivation
Instead of calculus, we can derive OLS purely using Linear Algebra & Vector Projections in observation space (\(\mathbb{R}^n\)):

Observation Space (\(\mathbb{R}^n\)): The target vector \(y \in \mathbb{R}^n\) lives in \(n\)-dimensional observation space (\(n=100\)). The origin \(\mathbf{0}\) represents zero response for all patients.
Model Subspace (\(\text{col}(X)\)): All possible predictions \(\hat{y}\) are linear combinations of the columns of \(X\): \[\begin{bmatrix} \hat{y}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}_n \end{bmatrix} = \theta_0 \mathbf{1}_n + \theta_1 \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{bmatrix}\] where \(\mathbf{1}_n\) denotes the \(n \times 1\) column vector of ones. All possible parameter combinations \((\theta_0, \theta_1)\) trace out the column space \(\text{col}(X)\), and any model prediction \(\hat{y}\) is simply an element of this subspace.
Orthogonal Projection: The point \(\hat{y} \in \text{col}(X)\) closest to \(y\) is the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto \(\text{col}(X)\).




Geometric Projection View of OLS




Orthogonality Condition
The residual error vector \(e = y - \hat{y} = y - X\hat{\theta}\) must drop at a right angle (\(\perp\)) onto \(\text{col}(X)\):
\[e \perp \text{col}(X) \iff X^T e = 0\]
Substituting \(e = y - X\hat{\theta}\):
\[X^T (y - X\hat{\theta}) = 0 \implies X^T y - X^T X \hat{\theta} = 0 \implies X^T X \hat{\theta} = X^T y\]

Conclusion: Both Calculus (\(\nabla_\theta \text{RSS} = 0\)) and Geometry (\(e \perp \text{col}(X)\)) yield the exact same Normal Equations!

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
6. Model Predictions
With the optimal parameters \(\hat \theta\), we can compute predicted responses \(\hat{y}\) for any patient data \(X\):
\[\hat{y} = X\hat{\theta} = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T y = H y \quad \text{where } H = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T\]

The Hat Matrix (\(H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\)): \(H\) transforms observed responses \(y\) directly into fitted predictions \(\hat{y}\) (“putting a hat on \(y\)”).
Projection Operator: The hat matrix \(H\) is symmetric (\(H^T = H\)) and acts as a projection operator that maps any vector from observation space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) onto the model subspace \(\text{col}(X)\), as illustrated in the geometric projection figure.

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
7. History of Regression
Behind every mathematical formula are historical pioneers, contextual motivations, and critical ethical reflections:



Historical Pioneers of Ordinary Least Squares: Carl Friedrich Gauss, Francis Galton, and Karl Pearson








WarningHistory and Ethics of Statistics




The Controversial Legacy: Both Francis Galton (who coined the term “eugenics”) and Karl Pearson (who held the Galton Chair of Eugenics at UCL) developed foundational statistical tools to quantify human genetics and social hierarchies.
Modern Data Science Lesson: Mathematics and algorithms are formal structures, but data selection, feature choice, and modeling goals are never strictly neutral. Understanding bias in statistical data is essential for responsible Machine Learning.

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
8. Summary

Matrix power: \(y = X\theta\)
Modesty: \(y = X\theta + e\)
Optimism:

\(e^T e \to \mbox{min}\)
\(e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\)
\(e \perp \hat{y}\)

Solution: \(\hat \theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\)
Predictions: \(\hat y = X \hat \theta\)
Projections: \(\hat y = H y\), where \(H = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T\) is the hat matrix: \(H = H^T = H^2\).

Model Spaces: Variables and Parameters
We distinguish between two complementary spaces:

Variable Space \((x, y)\): Each observation (e.g. patient) is a point \((x_i, y_i)\), and a candidate model is represented as a line \(\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\).
Parameter Space \((\theta_0, \theta_1)\): The space of model configurations. Each point \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_0, \theta_1)\) represents an entire candidate model. The loss function \(RSS(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) forms a convex quadratic bowl over this parameter plane.

NoteNotice




Regression Goal: \[RSS(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}))^2 = \mathbf{e}^T \mathbf{e} \to \min\]
Parameterized Models: Each parameter combination \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_0, \theta_1)\) corresponds to a specific (linear) model in variable space.
Loss Topography: Some models have a lower loss; For a given dataset (\(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}\)), the OLS solution \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\) sits precisely at the unique global minimum.
Samples May Need Selection: Sometimes samples have to be removed because of missing or wrongly annotated data.
Variables May Need Transformations: In this first example, insulin and glucose are plotted in their raw, untransformed clinical units, but sometimes feature transformations (e.g. \(\tilde{x} = \log(x)\)) could improve model fit and stabilize variance. See the Feature Engineering reference guide.
Parameter Interpretation: Parameters may carry units and meaning; intercept \(\theta_0\) is the baseline level at zero input, and the slope \(\theta_1\) is the expected response rate per unit increase in the predictor.
Even the Best Models Will Be Wrong: No straight line can fully capture true biological complexity.









ImportantSummary




For a given dataset we can find the optimal linear model: unique & deterministic
Model still has uncertainties due to:

sampling variability: parameter estimates
irreducible noise: residuals
systematic bias: model misspecification

Figure 1: Deviations from the truth arise as systematic errors (biases) and from sample-to-sample volatility (variance).







1.1 Decomposition of the Residual Error






NoteMathematical Setup & Random Variables











Quantity
Variable / Expression
Expectation & Properties




Truth
\(f(x)\)
\(\mathbb{E}[f(x)] = f(x)\) (unknown,deterministic function of \(x\) and possibly further variables)


Noise
\(\varepsilon\)
\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2] = \sigma^2\)


Observed Target
\(Y = f(x) + \varepsilon\)
\(\mathbb{E}[Y] = f(x) + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = f(x)\)


Model Prediction
\(\hat{Y}\)
\(\mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}]\) (expected model prediction across training datasets)


Residual Error
\(Y - \hat{Y}\)
\(\mathbb{E}[Y - \hat{Y}]\) (expected difference between target and prediction






Decomposition of the Residual Error
The residual error, \(Y - \hat{Y}\), is a random variable that can be decomposed into three distinct components: Bias, Variance, and Irreducible Noise:
\[\begin{aligned}
Y - \hat{Y} &= \big(f(x) + \varepsilon\big) - \hat{Y} \\
&= \underbrace{\big(f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}]\big)}_{B} + \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}] - \hat{Y}\big)}_{V} + \varepsilon \\
&= B + V + \varepsilon
\end{aligned}\]
where:

bias \(B = f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}]\) measures the systematic deviation between the true underlying mechanism \(f(x)\) and the expected prediction of the model across datasets. Notice that \(B\) is a deterministic constant.
variance \(V = \mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}] - \hat{Y}\) captures the sample-to-sample fluctuation of the estimator \(\hat{Y}\) around its own expectation (with \(\mathbb{E}[V] = 0\)).
\(\varepsilon = Y - f(x)\) is the irreducible noise in the target observation (with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\)).



Mean Squared Error and the Pythagorean Relation
The Mean Squared Error (MSE) is the expected squared residual error:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{MSE} & = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \hat{Y})^2]  \\
           & = \mathbb{E}\left[(B + V + \varepsilon)^2\right] \\
           & = \mathbb{E}[B^2] + \mathbb{E}[V^2] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2] \\
&\quad + 2\,\mathbb{E}[B V] + 2\,\mathbb{E}[B \varepsilon] + 2\,\mathbb{E}[V \varepsilon]
\end{aligned}\]
All three cross-terms vanish:

Bias and Variance: Because \(B\) is a deterministic constant, it factors out of the expectation: \[\mathbb{E}[B V] = B \cdot \mathbb{E}[V] = B \cdot \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}] - \hat{Y}] = B \cdot 0 = 0\]
Bias and Noise: Because \(B\) is constant and the noise has zero mean: \[\mathbb{E}[B \varepsilon] = B \cdot \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = B \cdot 0 = 0\]
Variance and Noise: Because the test noise \(\varepsilon\) is independent of the training data used to form \(\hat{Y}\): \[\mathbb{E}[V \varepsilon] = \mathbb{E}[V] \cdot \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0 \cdot 0 = 0\]







NotePythagoras again: Orthogonality of Random Variables



If we define the inner product of two random variables as \(\langle U, W \rangle = \mathbb{E}[U W]\), then \(\mathbb{E}[U W] = 0\) is equivalent to orthogonality of the two random variables. So the decomposition of the MSE is reminiscent of the Pythagorean theorem.


\[\boxed{\text{MSE} = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \hat{Y})^2] = \underbrace{(f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}])^2}_{\text{Bias}^2(\hat{Y})} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[(\hat{Y} - \mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}])^2\right]}_{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{Y})} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{Irreducible Noise}}}\]

title: 05 Linear Regression: Regularization
text:
2. \(L_2\) Regularization (Ridge)
Because irreducible noise \(\sigma^2\) is an unchangeable property, reducing total prediction error requires balancing Bias and Variance:

Standard OLS fits training data without constraints. For flexible models (such as high-degree polynomials), OLS achieves zero or near-zero training bias (\(\text{Bias}^2 \approx 0\)), but can result in large Variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{Y})\) where predictions swing wildly from one sample (e.g. patient cohort) to another.
The Regularization Principle: Rather than insisting on strict unbiasedness, the goal of regularization is to deliberately accept a small, controlled amount of Bias by constraining parameter magnitudes, in exchange for a large reduction in Variance.

By accepting a slight bias, we stabilize the estimator against sample-to-sample volatility and achieve a substantially lower overall Mean Squared Error.

2.1 The Ridge Estimator
Ridge Regression (\(L_2\) Regularization) operationalizes this principle by adding a penalty on the squared Euclidean norm of the parameter vector to the loss function:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2\]
where:

\(\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol{\theta})^2\) is the standard Residual Sum of Squares (RSS).
\(\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^p \theta_j^2\) is the squared Euclidean norm of the parameter vector.
\(\lambda \ge 0\) is the regularization hyperparameter:

\(\lambda = 0\): Recovers standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).
\(\lambda \to \infty\): Drives all weights toward zero (\(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \to \mathbf{0}\)).


Minimizing the regularized loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) yields the modified normal equations in closed form:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{Ridge}} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]
Notice the algebraic effect of \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\):

When model space is large, the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) is near-singular and poorly conditioned.
Adding \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) shifts every diagonal entry by \(+\lambda\), guaranteeing that \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\) is strictly positive-definite and invertible for any \(\lambda > 0\).

title: 05 Linear Regression: Regularization
text:
3. \(L_1\) Regularization (Lasso)
While Ridge shrinks coefficients continuously toward zero, it rarely drives any parameter strictly to zero. Lasso Regression (\(L_1\) Regularization) replaces the squared penalty with the sum of absolute values:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Lasso}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_1 = \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\theta_j|\]
Because the absolute value function \(|\theta_j|\) is non-differentiable at \(\theta_j = 0\), Lasso has no closed-form analytical solution and is solved numerically via coordinate descent.

3.1 Geometric Comparison of \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) Norms in 2D
To visualize why Lasso produces exact zeros (sparsity) while Ridge does not, consider all points in two dimensions at unit distance (\(\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\| = 1\)) from the origin:

\(L_2\) Norm Unit Contour: \(\{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \theta_1^2 + \theta_2^2 = 1\}\) forms a smooth circle.
\(L_1\) Norm Unit Contour: \(\{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |\theta_1| + |\theta_2| = 1\}\) forms a diamond with sharp corners at \((\pm 1, 0)\) and \((0, \pm 1)\) directly on the coordinate axes.



Generate 2D L1 vs. L2 Norm Comparison

# L2 Unit Circle
theta_angle = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 200)
axes[0].plot(np.cos(theta_angle), np.sin(theta_angle), color='#1f77b4', lw=2.5, label=r'$\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 = 1$')
axes[0].fill(np.cos(theta_angle), np.sin(theta_angle), color='#1f77b4', alpha=0.15)

Figure 2: Geometric Comparison of L1 and L2 Norms: All points at unit distance from zero in 2D. The L1 diamond has sharp vertices directly on the axes, promoting parameter sparsity, while the L2 circle is smooth everywhere.





When minimizing the loss subject to a budget constraint \(\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\| \le C\), the expanding elliptical contours of the RSS objective contact the diamond at its sharp coordinate axes first, forcing coordinates strictly to zero (\(\theta_j = 0\)).

title: 05 Linear Regression: Regularization
text:
4. Regularizing High-Degree Polynomials
To demonstrate how regularization tames extreme model flexibility, we revisit the Degree 15 polynomial on the 20 patient observations from Lecture 04:

4.1 Comparison of Fitted Parameter Weights: OLS, Ridge, and Lasso
To understand how regularization transforms model complexity, we inspect the learned parameter weights across all 16 polynomial terms (\(u^0, u^1, \dots, u^{15}\)), where \(u^0 = 1\) represents the intercept:

Unpenalized Intercept (\(u^0\)): In both Ridge and Lasso, the intercept \(\theta_0\) (\(u^0\)) is deliberately unpenalized, ensuring that the model remains invariant to constant vertical shifts in \(y\). Notice that \(u^0\) remains active across all four models, anchoring the prediction to the mean level of the observations.
Ordinary Least Squares (\(\lambda = 0\)): Without regularization, the unconstrained estimator fits sample noise, driving adjacent monomial weights into opposing billions (\(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\|_2 \approx 1.83 \times 10^{10}\)), identical to the weight explosion seen in Lecture 04.
Ridge Regularization (\(\lambda = 0.1\)): The \(L_2\) penalty continuously shrinks all 15 feature weights simultaneously by nine orders of magnitude (\(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\|_2 \approx 9.27\)). Crucially, all 16 parameters remain non-zero—Ridge achieves shrinkage, not sparsity.
Lasso Regularization (\(\lambda = 10^{-3}\), Mild): Because the \(L_1\) diamond ball has sharp corners aligned with the coordinate axes, Lasso drives redundant coefficients strictly to zero. At mild penalty, 11 of the 15 feature powers are pruned to zero, leaving active weights on the intercept \(u^0\) and the low-degree terms (\(u^1, u^2, u^3\)) that capture the underlying parabolic signal.
Lasso Regularization (\(\lambda = 0.1\), Strong): At the exact same regularization strength as Ridge (\(\lambda = 0.1\)), Lasso sets 13 of the 15 feature weights to exactly zero, isolating only the intercept \(u^0\) and the dominant curvature features (\(u^2\) and \(u^3\)).

title: 05 Linear Regression: Regularization
text:
5. Summary & Key Takeaways

Residual Error Decomposition: Total Mean Squared Error decomposes into \(\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2\) because the bias vector \(\mathbf{v}_{\text{bias}}\), variance vector \(\mathbf{v}_{\text{var}}\), and noise vector \(\varepsilon\) are mutually orthogonal in expectation.
\(L_2\) Regularization (Ridge): Adds \(\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2\) to the loss, continuously shrinking parameter weights and shifting the Gram matrix eigenvalues to guarantee invertibility \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\).
\(L_1\) Regularization (Lasso): Adds \(\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_1\), leveraging the sharp corners of the diamond unit ball to perform automatic feature selection by setting uninformative weights strictly to zero.
Controlling High Degrees: Regularization allows us to use rich hypothesis spaces (such as high-degree polynomials) while completely preventing the explosive oscillations characteristic of unconstrained Ordinary Least Squares.

4. Theory: Summary
Recap: [Uniform distributions, CDFs, change of variables]

Linear Congruential Generator (LCG): \[X_{n+1} = (a X_n + c) \bmod m\]
Inverse Transform Sampling: \[X = F^{-1}(U), \quad U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)\]
Rejection Sampling Acceptance Condition: \[U \le \frac{p(Y)}{M \cdot q(Y)}, \quad Y \sim q(y)\]
Metropolis-Hastings Acceptance Ratio: \[\alpha(x, x') = \min\left(1, \frac{\tilde{p}(x') q(x|x')}{\tilde{p}(x) q(x'|x)}\right)\]

5. Implementations and Illustrations
Metropolis-Hastings MCMC implementation:
import numpy as np

# Metropolis-Hastings for target p(x) ~ exp(-0.5 * x^2)
def metropolis_hastings(n_samples=5000, width=0.5):
    samples = np.zeros(n_samples)
    curr = 0.0
    for i in range(1, n_samples):
        prop = curr + np.random.normal(0, width)
        ratio = np.exp(-0.5 * prop**2) / np.exp(-0.5 * curr**2)
        if np.random.rand() < min(1.0, ratio):
            curr = prop
        samples[i] = curr
    return samples

text:
Task 1: Streamlined Data Preparation
A sound classification workflow requires rigorous data preparation before mathematical estimation:

Target Encoding: In Scikit-Learn’s raw dataset, target is encoded as 0 = Malignant and 1 = Benign. In clinical diagnostic screening, the positive class (\(y = 1\)) conventionally represents the presence of pathology (Malignant). Define: \[y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Malignant} \\ 0 & \text{if Benign} \end{cases}\]
Class Imbalance Audit: Calculate the sample counts and empirical prevalence: \[\text{Prevalence} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\] Reflection: If an uneducated baseline model simply predicts “Benign” for every patient, what accuracy would it achieve? Why does class imbalance make naive accuracy a treacherous metric?
Stratified Partitioning: Split the dataset into 80% training (\(n_{\text{train}} = 455\)) and 20% test (\(n_{\text{test}} = 114\)) subsets using stratify=y to preserve exact class proportions in both sets.
Feature Standardization (\(Z\)-scoring): Standardize all 30 predictors by centering to zero mean and scaling to unit variance: \[z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j}{s_j}\] Methodological Rule: Fit the StandardScaler strictly on the training partition, then transform both training and test partitions to prevent data leakage.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
section: Task 2: Linear Regression Baseline & Exposing Its Failure Modes
text:
Task 2: Linear Regression Baseline & Exposing Its Failure Modes
Before implementing logistic regression, we examine what happens if we apply Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression—the Linear Probability Model (LPM)—directly to a qualitative binary target: \[y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\theta} + \varepsilon_i, \quad y_i \in \{0, 1\}\]

Bivariate OLS Fit: Select a prominent morphological predictor, worst concave points (\(x\)), and fit a simple 1D linear regression model \(\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\).
Visualizing the Linear Probability Fit: Plot the fitted line \(\hat{y}(x)\) against the binary scatter points \(y \in \{0, 1\}\).
Failure Mode 1 (Out-of-Bounds Predictions): Identify data points where the linear model predicts \(\hat{y} < 0\) or \(\hat{y} > 1\). Conceptual Question: What does a predicted probability of \(\hat{y} = -0.15\) or \(\hat{y} = 1.25\) mean clinically? Why does this violate Kolmogorov’s probability axioms?
Failure Mode 2 (Extreme Outlier Distortion): Introduce a hypothetical patient with an extremely high biomarker value (\(x = 6.0\), clearly malignant \(y=1\)). Refit the OLS model. Observe how squared error \((y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\) severely penalizes this extreme point even though it is correctly classified, tilting the line and shifting the decision threshold (\(\hat{y} = 0.5\)), which misclassifies borderline patients.
Failure Mode 3 (Violation of Gauss-Markov Homoscedasticity): In OLS, we assume \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2\). However, for a Bernoulli variable \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) with conditional expectation \(p(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\): \[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) = p(x)(1 - p(x)) = (\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\theta})(1 - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\theta})\] The variance inherently varies with \(x\), completely invalidating standard OLS hypothesis testing and standard errors.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
section: Task 3: The Logistic Link Function & Multivariable Fitting
text:
Task 3: The Logistic Link Function & Multivariable Fitting
To resolve the fatal flaws of the Linear Probability Model, we model the probability via a smooth non-linear mapping from \(\mathbb{R} \to (0, 1)\):

Mathematical Formulation

Linear Predictor: \[z_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\theta} = \theta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^p \theta_j z_{ij}\]
Sigmoid Activation (Logistic Link): \[\hat{p}_i = P(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma(z_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_i}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\theta}}}\] The sigmoid function satisfies \(\lim_{z \to -\infty} \sigma(z) = 0\) and \(\lim_{z \to +\infty} \sigma(z) = 1\), strictly bounding predictions in \((0, 1)\) while plateauting for extreme confident values.
Log-Odds (Logit): \[\ln\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right) = z_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\theta}\]
Binary Cross-Entropy Loss (Negative Log-Likelihood): \[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \ln(\hat{p}_i) + (1 - y_i) \ln(1 - \hat{p}_i) \right]\]
Gradient Link to Ordinary Least Squares: \[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{X}^T (\hat{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{y})\] Notice the structural parallel to the OLS normal equation gradient \(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^T(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})\). Because \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}\) is a non-linear function of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), there is no closed-form solution \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^Ty\); the optimum must be found iteratively using Newton-Raphson or L-BFGS.


Model Fitting: Fit an unregularized multivariable logistic regression model using all 30 standardized predictors (penalty=None).

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
text:
Task 4: Parameter Interpretation & Odds Ratios
In linear regression, \(\theta_j\) is the additive change in \(y\) per unit change in \(x_j\). In logistic regression:
\[\ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \dots + \theta_j x_j + \dots + \theta_p x_p\]
Exponentiating both sides yields the multiplicative Odds Ratio (OR): \[\frac{p}{1-p} = e^{\theta_0} \cdot e^{\theta_1 x_1} \dots e^{\theta_j x_j}\] \[\text{OR}_j = \frac{\text{Odds}(x_j + 1)}{\text{Odds}(x_j)} = e^{\theta_j}\]

Interpretation: Because features were standardized (\(Z\)-scores), a 1 standard deviation increase in feature \(x_j\) multiplies the odds of malignancy by \(\exp(\theta_j)\), holding all other features fixed.

If \(\theta_j > 0 \implies \text{OR}_j > 1\): the biomarker increases the risk of malignancy.
If \(\theta_j < 0 \implies \text{OR}_j < 1\): the biomarker decreases the risk of malignancy.
If \(\theta_j = 0 \implies \text{OR}_j = 1\): the feature has no predictive association.

Multicollinearity Audit: Examine the coefficient magnitudes in the plot below. Notice how strongly correlated features (e.g. radius_worst, perimeter_worst, area_worst) display huge opposing positive and negative coefficients.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
section: Task 5: Decision Boundaries, Thresholds & Clinical Diagnostics
text:
Task 5: Decision Boundaries, Thresholds & Clinical Diagnostics
A probabilistic classifier outputs \(\hat{p}_i \in [0, 1]\). To make clinical treatment decisions, continuous probabilities are mapped to discrete classes via a decision threshold \(t \in [0, 1]\): \[\hat{y}_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \hat{p}_i \ge t \\ 0 & \text{if } \hat{p}_i < t \end{cases}\]

Clinical Evaluation Metrics
From the \(2 \times 2\) Confusion Matrix: * Sensitivity (Recall / True Positive Rate): \(\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}\) — The fraction of malignant tumors correctly flagged. * Specificity (True Negative Rate): \(\text{TNR} = \frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FP}}\) — The fraction of benign tumors correctly cleared. * Precision (Positive Predictive Value): \(\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}\) — The probability that a flagged patient truly has malignancy.






NoteAsymmetric Clinical Costs in Oncology



In cancer screening, diagnostic errors are not symmetrical: * False Negative (FN): A malignant tumor is missed. Disease progresses untreated, potentially resulting in patient mortality. * False Positive (FP): A benign tumor is flagged as malignant. The patient experiences psychological distress and undergoes an unnecessary confirmation biopsy. Because a False Negative is far more dangerous than a False Positive, clinical screening protocols often lower the decision threshold (\(t < 0.5\)) to maximize Sensitivity.



Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve: Plot Sensitivity (TPR) vs. \(1 - \text{Specificity}\) (FPR) across all thresholds \(t \in [0, 1]\).
Area Under the Curve (AUC): Measures the probability that the model ranks a randomly chosen malignant patient higher than a randomly chosen benign patient.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
text:
Task 6: Multicollinearity Pathology & Overfitting Audit
In Task 4, we observed that unregularized logistic regression produced massive, opposing parameter estimates. Why does this happen?

Severe Collinearity in Cell Morphology: Cell radius (\(r\)), perimeter (\(p \approx 2\pi r\)), and area (\(a \approx \pi r^2\)) are bound by fundamental geometric relations. Their correlation exceeds \(r > 0.99\).
Matrix Conditioning: In logistic regression, parameter covariance is governed by the inverse of the weighted Gram matrix (Hessian): \[\mathbf{H} = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{X}, \quad \text{where } \mathbf{W} = \operatorname{diag}(\hat{p}_i(1 - \hat{p}_i))\] When features are collinear, \(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{X}\) is near-singular (\(\det \to 0\)), driving parameter variances \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}_j) \to \infty\).
The Regularized Optimization Framework: To tame parameter explosion, we augment the objective with a penalty \(\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\): \[\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} C \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\] where \(C = \frac{1}{\lambda}\) is Scikit-Learn’s inverse regularization parameter:

Large \(C\) (\(\lambda \to 0\)): Weak penalty \(\to\) approaches unconstrained maximum likelihood.
Small \(C\) (\(\lambda \to \infty\)): Heavy penalty \(\to\) forces coefficients toward zero.
Convention: The intercept \(\theta_0\) is unpenalized so the model can freely adjust baseline class prevalence.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
text:
Task 7: Ridge (\(L_2\)) Regularization: Smooth Shrinkage
Ridge regression adds the squared Euclidean norm of the weight vector to the loss:
\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1:p}\|_2^2 = \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \sum_{j=1}^p \theta_j^2\]

Key Algebraic & Geometric Properties:

Hessian Stabilization: The Hessian becomes \(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{ridge}} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I}\). Adding positive \(\lambda\) to the diagonal shifts all eigenvalues upward, guaranteeing strict positive definiteness and non-singular inversion.
Smooth Shrinkage: Large parameter magnitudes are heavily penalized, shrinking weights continuously toward zero without setting any weight exactly to zero.
Collinearity Handling: When two features are nearly identical (\(x_1 \approx x_2\)), Ridge encourages them to share equal weights (\(\theta_1 \approx \theta_2\)), preventing the explosive \(\pm\) cancellations seen in OLS.


Fit a Ridge logistic regression model with \(C = 1.0\) and compare coefficient magnitudes against the unregularized model.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
section: Task 8: Lasso (\(L_1\)) Regularization: Sparsity & Biomarker Selection
text:
Task 8: Lasso (\(L_1\)) Regularization: Sparsity & Biomarker Selection
Lasso replaces the \(L_2\) sum of squares with the \(L_1\) sum of absolute values:
\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1:p}\|_1 = \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\theta_j|\]

Geometric Mechanism of Sparsity

The constraint region for \(L_1\) is a diamond/octahedron with sharp corners located on the coordinate axes.
The elliptical loss contours of \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) expand outward and typically hit a corner of the \(L_1\) diamond first.
At a corner, one or more coordinate axes have \(\theta_j \equiv 0\).
Consequently, Lasso performs automated feature selection, pruning redundant variables and extracting a sparse biomarker signature.
Fit a Lasso model with \(C = 0.5\) using the saga solver (which supports \(L_1\) optimization) and count the number of non-zero features.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
section: Task 9: Visualizing Regularization Paths Across 6 Orders of Magnitude
text:
Task 9: Visualizing Regularization Paths Across 6 Orders of Magnitude
To understand how penalty strength controls model flexibility, we compute the regularization path: tracking the trajectory of all 30 weights \(\theta_j(C)\) as \(C\) ranges from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{3}\):

Path Computation: Generate 50 logarithmically spaced values: C_vals = np.logspace(-4, 3, 50). Fit both Ridge and Lasso at each \(C\) and record all coefficients.
Ridge Paths: Observe smooth continuous decay toward zero; all 30 lines shrink, but none equal zero.
Lasso Paths: Observe piecewise-linear paths where features hit zero sequentially at distinct critical thresholds.
Sparsity Profile: Plot the number of active features (\(k\)) as a function of \(\log_{10}(C)\).

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
text:
Task 10: 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation & Hyperparameter Tuning
We cannot pick the optimal penalty \(C\) using training accuracy, because training performance improves monotonically as \(C \to \infty\) (overfitting). Instead, we employ \(K\)-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation to optimize out-of-sample diagnostic ability (ROC-AUC):

Partition the training set into \(K = 5\) stratified folds.
Evaluate performance across the grid of candidate values \(C\).
Select \(C^*\) that maximizes cross-validated ROC-AUC.
Identify which core biomarkers survive in the optimal Lasso model.

title: Tutorial 04a: Logistic Regression & Regularization (Lasso & Ridge)
section: Task 11: Final Out-of-Sample Evaluation & Model Critique
text:
Task 11: Final Out-of-Sample Evaluation & Model Critique
We now perform a comprehensive head-to-head comparison on the held-out 20% test partition (\(n_{\text{test}} = 114\) patients never seen during training or cross-validation):

Linear Probability Model (LPM): Thresholded at \(\hat{y} = 0.5\).
Unregularized Logistic Regression: Maximum likelihood with all 30 features.
Tuned Ridge Logistic Regression: \(L_2\) regularization with optimal \(C^*_{\text{ridge}}\).
Tuned Lasso Logistic Regression: \(L_1\) regularization with optimal \(C^*_{\text{lasso}}\).


Evaluation Criteria:

Test Accuracy: Proportion of correct classifications at threshold \(0.5\).
Test ROC-AUC: Diagnostic ranking capability independent of threshold.
Test Log-Loss (BCE): Penalizes confident wrong probability predictions.
Active Features (\(k\)): Clinical simplicity and cost of implementation.







NoteClinical Verdict: The Value of Sparsity



While both Ridge and Lasso achieve exceptional test performance, the Tuned Lasso model achieves parity using only a fraction of the original features. In an operational pathology laboratory, acquiring and validating 30 separate nuclear measurements requires significant imaging software overhead; a streamlined panel of key biomarkers simplifies the diagnostic assay, speeds turnaround times, and provides transparent clinical interpretability.









NoteConceptual Review Questions






Linear Regression Failure Modes: Explain three distinct mathematical reasons why Ordinary Least Squares with squared error loss \((y - \hat{y})^2\) fails when applied to a binary health classification task (\(y \in \{0, 1\}\)).
Geometry of Sparsity: Geometrically explain why \(L_1\) (Lasso) regularization forces parameter weights strictly to zero (\(\theta_j \equiv 0\)), whereas \(L_2\) (Ridge) regularization shrinks weights smoothly without setting them exactly to zero.
The Role of Feature Standardization: Why is predictor standardization (\(Z\)-scoring) mandatory before fitting Ridge or Lasso models, whereas in unregularized Ordinary Least Squares it simply rescales the parameter vector without affecting model fit or predictions?

title: Correlations
text:
Variable Relationships
To quantify associations between paired continuous variables, we evaluate two complementary correlation measures:

Pearson Correlation Coefficient (\(r_{xy} \in [-1, 1]\)): Measures strictly linear association: \[r_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(x, y)}{s_x s_y}\] In vector form with mean-centered vectors \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} - \bar{x}\mathbf{1}\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\): \[r_{xy} = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^T \tilde{\mathbf{y}}}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\|_2 \|\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\|_2} = \cos(\phi)\]
Spearman Rank Correlation (\(r_s \in [-1, 1]\)): Evaluates monotonic association by computing Pearson’s formula on the ranks \(R(x)\) and \(R(y)\): \[r_s = 1 - \frac{6 \sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2}{n(n^2 - 1)}, \qquad d_i = R(x_i) - R(y_i)\] Spearman’s \(r_s\) assesses whether variables increase together regardless of whether the trend is linear, and is substantially more robust to extreme outliers.



Code
x = df_clean['insulin']
y = df_clean['glucose']
r_pearson = x.corr(y, method='pearson')
r_spearman = x.corr(y, method='spearman')

NotePearson versus Spearman




Sensitivity to High-Leverage Outliers: Pearson correlation operates on squared Euclidean distances. Extreme insulin observations (reaching up to \(846\ \mu\text{U/ml}\)) pull on the linear fit and attenuate sample covariance.
Biological Saturation: Cellular glucose response naturally exhibits saturation (diminishing return at high insulin concentrations). Rank transformation straightens monotonic curvature, bounding extreme outliers and capturing the true strength of biological co-regulation.
Attention — Single Summary Metrics: Both numbers are just single scalar values attempting to summarize potentially complex bivariate data structures. Neither number should be considered “true”, and both have distinct limitations:

Ties and excessive zeros: When datasets contain many identical zero values (e.g., missing records, detection limits, or single-cell dropouts), rank assignment can heavily skew Spearman’s rank correlation.
Isolated extreme outliers: A single extreme bivariate outlier can heavily inflate or deflate sample covariance, creating the illusion of a very strong or falsely absent Pearson correlation. Always inspect the bivariate scatter plot rather than relying blindly on a single correlation coefficient.

TipLink to Multicollinearity in Regression



When two predictor columns exhibit high pairwise correlation (\(|r| \approx 1\)), their columns in the design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) are nearly linearly dependent. This causes the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) to approach singularity (\(\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) \approx 0\)), inflating parameter estimation variance in \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\).
